visible.name: Ravi Menon
visible.line: Ravi Menon, 27, is a fourth-year machine learning PhD student who works on making pretraining cheaper, and he is preparing a conference paper on pruning training data early in a run.

project.title: Prune Early
project.logline: An empirical paper showing that dropping a third of the training data early in pretraining matches full-data quality at about a third less compute, tested at two model scales.
constraints: The conference deadline is in three weeks and the paper is limited to nine pages plus an appendix.
The lab allows eight GPUs for about six days per week of runs.
Every main result needs at least three seeds, and the group's rule is five.
One strong baseline needs two days of compute and its code is hard to run.
The advisor wants a one-page results sheet every Monday.

tone_requests.text: Be terse and put the numbers first.
Give me a table when comparing more than two things.
Don't explain basics; I know the field.
Tell me what you would run to check it.

stated_views.text: A claim without an ablation is a hunch.
If it only works at one scale, it is not a result yet.
Reviewers reward big tables more than clever arguments.
Theory that doesn't change what you run is decoration.

plans.text: On Day 3 I'm launching the 120-run sweep on the lab's eight GPUs.
On Day 6 I'm sending the advisor the one-page results sheet.
On Day 10 I'm giving a fifteen-minute talk at the lab meeting.

new_work.text: I'm writing the related-work section for my paper on pruning training data early in pretraining. I have 14 papers: six on data selection, four on curriculum, four on scaling laws. I'd like a table by what each measured. Does that structure work?
Here's my experiment plan for next week: five seeds, three pruning ratios, two model sizes, four data mixes. That's 120 runs and I have 8 GPUs for 6 days. Is that too much or should I cut the mixes?

Reviewer 2 wrote: "The improvement from pruning may come from the learning-rate schedule rather than the pruned data." I have a new ablation that holds the schedule fixed. How should I answer in under 500 words?

I need a poster abstract of 150 words for the workshop. The headline is that pruning 30 percent of data at step 2,000 matches the full-data baseline at one-third of the compute. How should I start it?
I'm building a 15-minute talk outline for a lab meeting. I have the method, three results slides and an ablation table. Should I spend the time on the method or the table?
My main table has 12 rows and the difference between the best two methods is 0.3 points with a standard deviation of 0.2. How should I word the claim in the abstract?
A coauthor suggests we add a theory section that explains why pruning helps. I don't have a proof and the deadline is in nine days. Should I add a hand-waving paragraph or leave it out?
I'm picking baselines for the data-pruning paper: random pruning, loss-based pruning, a learned scorer and a recent method whose code needs two days to run. Do I include the last one?
Here's the paper's title: "Prune Early: Matching Full-Data Pretraining at a Third of the Compute." A friend says it's too long. Should I shorten it?
The ablation on pruning ratio at the larger model shows a drop at 50 percent that doesn't appear at the smaller one. Do I report it, rerun it, or drop that row?
I have to decide whether to submit to the big conference deadline in three weeks or to a smaller workshop next month. The main result holds at two scales but not three. Which one?
I'm writing the limitations paragraph. I know the result was only tested on one data mix at the large scale. How blunt should I be?
My advisor wants a one-page results sheet for Monday. I have the main table, one ablation and two plots. What should go on the page?
A reviewer says my code release is "hard to run." I have a single config file and a 200-line README. What's the quickest thing to improve?
I'm reproducing a baseline from another group's paper and my numbers are two points below theirs. Should I report mine, theirs, or both?
I need to turn the three-seed result into a five-seed one before submission, but a node is down. Can I report three seeds with a note?
I'm writing the first sentence of the introduction: "Data pruning is popular but understudied." Is that a good opening, or should I start with a number?
A junior student asked what to run on their first day. I have a list of ten sweeps. Which should I give them?
I've found a bug in the data loader that duplicated 1 percent of the examples in the pruned runs. The headline result may shift by 0.2. What do I do first?
I'm designing Figure 1. I'd like the main curve of loss versus compute for pruned and full data with a shaded band. Should I add a second panel for the ablation?
The workshop asks for a four-page version. I have eight pages. What gets cut first?
I'm drafting the acknowledgements. I want to thank the compute provider and two labmates who found the bug. How should I word it?
A colleague says the paper's claims are too narrow for the big venue. I think precise is better. How do I decide?
I have a talk invitation in four weeks at a reading group. Should I give the paper talk or a talk on the lessons from the failed ablations?
I'm choosing which of the three figures to put in the main text. They are the compute curve, the pruning-ratio ablation and the data-mix heatmap. Which two?
I'm planning the next three months. I can follow up on pruning with a bigger model or switch to a new problem on curriculum. Which is better for my thesis?
